podcast.body: A more rock-forward album, also produced by Tony Visconti, recorded with the intention of giving Bowie's touring band more live material for his upcoming tour. While its lead single "New Killer Star" didn't chart anywhere, the album itself did solid business, making the top 30 in America and the top 3 in the UK, leading to his extensive Reality Tour. "Bowie and Visconti kept the momentum going with 2003's more rock-forward reality, an album they recorded with the intention of giving Bowie's touring band more live material."

podcast.body: Bowie was touring this album in 2004 during what was reported as a very happy period in his life, shortly before he suffered a heart attack on stage. "Bowie was on his reality tour and things were going well. Bowie was reported to be happier than he'd been a long time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Following "Heathen," this album further demonstrated Bowie's continued commitment to making music into the 21st century. It seemed to indicate that he planned to keep recording indefinitely. "And then reality from 2003, and it looked like Bowie had every intention of never stopping."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Released in 2003, this album was supported by what would become Bowie's last large-scale road trip. The tour ended early due to his health problems. "There was a tour for his next album, Reality, which appeared in 2003. But it would be his last large-scale road trip."

podcast.body: This album, part of Bowie's later career, had its musical quality questioned prior to the posthumous success and critical re-evaluation that followed Black Star's release. "los últimos albumes de la carrera de David Bowie sobre todo los últimos tres, cuatro albumes, el hitin, el hours, el reality, habían sido un tanto cuestionado por su calidad musical."
